perspective:
I, Carolyn Abebe, have access to the following information:

- I am a bank teller at a community bank. Marilyn Olson is my colleague; we recently started working together and are still getting to know each other.
- During a busy week with increased customer traffic and stress, I noticed Marilyn was unusually quiet and withdrawn, unlike her normally engaging demeanor. I asked if she was all right and whether she wanted to talk. She told me she was overwhelmed with work and some personal stuff, and thanked me for asking.
- In a later interaction, Marilyn was curt with me. I felt confused and slightly hurt. I told her I hoped I hadn’t overstepped, that I’d had tough times too, and that talking sometimes helps. She said she appreciated it, apologized if she seemed off, and said it had been a hard week for her.
- After that, Marilyn appeared to respond positively. I felt relieved and hopeful about our friendship. I invited her to a small get-together with friends that weekend. She said it sounded lovely, thanked me, and accepted.
- Despite friendly interactions outside work, I felt Marilyn was still maintaining a professional distance at the bank. I felt disappointed and asked to talk about our work dynamic, saying I sensed a distance I couldn’t understand. She said she didn’t realize that, was sorry if it seemed that way, and agreed to talk about improving our collaboration.
- After our private meeting, I believed we had cleared the air and better understood each other’s professional expectations and personal boundaries. I felt content and optimistic. I proposed teaming up for the new project proposal. She agreed, said she was glad we had the talk, and said she looked forward to working more closely with me.

I do not have access to Marilyn’s private reasons beyond what she told me, her internal thoughts or feelings, or any hidden information about why she behaved as she did.
